title: AI's real value in healthcare isn't diagnosis—it's catching traps in contracts
dek: Healthcare giants hide price increases through thousands of shell companies, but once you sign, AI can't save you—the only answer is to feed your contract to AI before signing and ask: where's the trap?
why: Breaks down how health giants bury money through subsidiaries and thousand-page contracts, explains what AI can and cannot do before and after signing, and speaks directly to anyone managing benefit costs.
who: HR and CFOs managing self-insured employee health plans, healthcare founders, investors asking which part of traditional industries AI actually fixes.
skip: The middle section on Epic, the EHR vendor, adds little—skip it.

points.h: Health giants hide billions through thousands of shell companies
points.body: Cuban notes UnitedHealth operates 3,000-plus subsidiaries with ~$150 billion in annual internal transfers—comparable to the 14th-largest state economy in the US. He explains how giants simultaneously raise premiums and deductibles while steering patients to undisclosed affiliates they own, generating extra profit through this structure.

points.h: Long contracts leave AI helpless after you sign
points.body: Cuban argues the problem isn't technology but the contracts themselves—a Dallas PBM agreement spans 1,335 pages, and no amount of human effort can extract every hidden trap. He stresses that once you sign, AI is nearly powerless; its true value lies in pre-signature review, preventing you from signing a bad deal in the first place.

points.h: Widespread AI contract review could collapse the whole system
points.body: Cuban calculates that more than 155 million Americans get coverage through employer plans—over 60% of the country. If those employers used AI to review contracts before signing, asking where the traps are, the entire BUCA and PBM system would collapse from losing its information advantage, and healthcare costs would crater.

points.h: Shrinking drug manufacturing from warehouses to shipping containers
points.body: Cost Plus Drugs has already compressed what once required a football-field-sized manufacturing line into a truck-sized pod, swapping drug batches every 4 hours using AI and robotics. Each pod costs ~$20 million; government is the first customer. Cuban aims to move hundreds in two years, thousands in five—he jokes that selling $20 billion in pods annually would make even Musk nervous.

points.h: Personalized drug design will trend toward zero cost
points.body: As large language models improve, Cuban expects the cost to design personalized drugs based on your DNA—even over-the-counter medications like ibuprofen—will fall toward zero. He suggests labs bundle this into subscription services the way 23andMe offers DNA testing for under $99, letting marginal costs spread across the user base.

points.h: AI makes medical patents harder to defend
points.body: Cuban raises an underexplored tension: if doctors and researchers use AI to generate new therapies, the ideal of free information collides with IP holders' real interests. He foresees closed licensing models where you pay per inference using someone's model—complicating access to the data needed for training and reasoning.

points.h: Replace employee health premiums with personal savings accounts
points.body: If advising the president, Cuban would replace insurance with savings: employers deposit the equivalent of an ACA Silver-plan premium into individual accounts, banks extend credit, government guarantees coverage, and federal stop-loss kicks in above the limit. If you never claim, retirement brings the balance plus interest—yours to keep. Unlike today's premiums, which you pay forever without benefit and still must fight to use.

points.h: Only two kinds of companies will exist: good at AI and bankrupt
points.body: Closing, Cuban says companies split into two camps: those adept with AI and those going bankrupt. Most founders are stuck at the stage of not daring to talk to AI—like fearing Lotus 1-2-3 spreadsheets back in the day. Whoever gets comfortable first spots opportunities no one else sees yet, including the basement-bound solo founders Cuban says will become trillion-dollar builders.
